summary: Operators using the RPKI issue Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs) to say which autonomous systems may originate BGP routes for their address blocks. This best-practice document discusses operational problems when one ROA lists several prefixes. It recommends that each ROA contain just one IP prefix.

eli5.summary: If one permission slip covers many things and one of them goes wrong, the whole slip stops working. This advice says to use one slip per thing, so a problem hurts less.

questions: should a roa contain multiple prefixes
what is fate sharing in rpki
why use one prefix per roa
subtitle: Why each RPKI route authorization should cover one IP prefix, so one problem does not take down the rest.

tldr.problem: A ROA with several IP prefixes is either valid or invalid as a whole, so unrelated routes share fate. A certificate change, an expiry or a reissuance for one prefix can invalidate the others.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends that, unless the CA has good reasons to the contrary, an issued ROA SHOULD contain a single IP prefix.
tldr.outcome: Single-prefix ROAs avoid fate-sharing, at the cost of more files for relying parties to fetch.

facts.label: Recommendation
facts.value: A ROA SHOULD contain a single IP prefix

today: RFC 9455 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 238) and, per the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: What a ROA Contains
sections.content:
In the RPKI, a ROA is a digitally signed object. It says that a single AS has been authorized by the address space holder to originate BGP routes to one or more IP prefixes within that address space (RFC 6482).

Each ROA has an asID field, holding one AS number, and an ipAddrBlocks field, holding one or more prefixes. To authorize more than one AS for the same prefixes, the holder must issue one ROA per AS number (RFC 6480).

Before this document there was no guidance on whether to issue a separate ROA for each prefix or one ROA containing several.
sections.eli5: A ROA is a signed note saying which network may announce which addresses. One note can list one address block or many, and nobody had said which is better.

sections.title: The Fate-Sharing Problem
sections.content:
A holder can issue a ROA per routing announcement, or one ROA for several announcements, or even for all of them under a given asID. A ROA is either valid or invalid, so every announcement it covers shares fate in RPKI validation. The RFC notes that no existing RFC discussed this.

The text gives three concrete ways this hurts.

  • A parent CA can revoke a delegated certificate at any time, changing its resources. Any ROA with resources no longer entirely inside the new certificate, or inside a certificate the relying party has not yet discovered, is rejected. Unchanged prefixes in that ROA fall with it.
  • A ROA has a single expiration time, so it affects all its prefixes. Changes for one prefix must be synchronized with the others.
  • If a prefix is authorized only for a period, for example when leased out temporarily, or routing changes for a subset of prefixes, reissuing a multi-prefix ROA is harder and more error-prone. It can change the validity of previously received BGP routes it covers.
sections.eli5: Imagine one ticket that covers five rides. If the ticket expires or tears, you lose all five rides, even if only one ride had a problem.

sections.title: Coordination Burden on CAs
sections.content:
CAs have to carefully coordinate ROA updates with updates to a resource certificate. This can be automated when a single entity manages both the parent CA and the CA issuing the ROAs (Scenario D in RFC 8211, Section 3.4). In other deployment scenarios the coordination becomes more complex.

With separate ROAs, each ROA has its own validity interval. Invalidity is then affected only by reissuance of the specific issuing parent CA certificate.
sections.eli5: Keeping many things on one form means everyone must agree before any change. Separate forms let each be changed on its own schedule.

sections.title: The Recommendation
sections.content:
The recommendation is one sentence: unless the CA has good reasons to the contrary, an issued ROA SHOULD contain a single IP prefix.

Using a ROA with a single prefix minimizes the side effects above. It avoids fate-sharing whatever the cause, provided the parent CA issuing each ROA remains valid and each ROA itself remains valid. Because it is a SHOULD, a CA with a good reason can still issue multi-prefix ROAs.

The document is a Best Current Practice (BCP 238) and defines no new protocol elements.
sections.eli5: The advice is simple: one note for each address block, unless you have a good reason not to.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content: The only cost the RFC names is that issuing separate ROAs for independent prefixes may increase the file-fetch burden on the relying party during validation. There are no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: More small notes means the checker has more papers to pick up and read.
